passage:
Tuesday night.

Signed the form today. Economics honours. It's official, no more "maybe biology, maybe design, maybe law" every week.

Bhupen asked me at lunch, "Aadhya, why so pale?" Honestly, I was scared. Choosing one thing means letting the others go. I kept thinking of the plant-cell diagrams I used to love, and my sketchbook from Class 11.

But when I sat in that economics intro class last month, the lecturer explained why onion prices jump every year and something clicked. I stayed back for an hour asking questions. I haven't felt that curious in ages.

So yes. Economics. I'll keep drawing for myself. Maybe I'll mix it in somehow later.

Mummy cried a little on the phone. Happy tears, I think. I'm still a bit wobbly but mostly excited. 😊

qa.q: What subject did Aadhya sign up for?
qa.a: Economics honours.

qa.q: Why was Aadhya scared when signing the form?
qa.a: Committing to economics meant letting go of other interests Aadhya loved, like biology and drawing.

qa.q: What would you advise Aadhya while settling into the course?
qa.a: Keep following the curiosity that made Aadhya stay back after class, and keep drawing on the side so that part isn't lost.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Aadhya's choice?
qa.a: Bhupen noticed the pale face, so may be concerned but also glad Aadhya finally made a decision after swinging every week.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows a student committing to a specific major and the mixed feelings that come with it.

passage:
Vandana: I did it. I enrolled at the ITI for the electrician course.
Sunaina: WAIT. what about the BA seat??
Vandana: I let it go. I sat through 3 weeks of BA classes and felt nothing
Vandana: then I helped my uncle rewire his shop and it was like my brain lit up
Sunaina: that's actually amazing
Sunaina: how did your parents take it
Vandana: Mummy is worried people will talk. "a girl climbing poles"
Vandana: Papa just said "if you're sure, finish it properly"
Sunaina: are you sure?
Vandana: yes. scared but yes
Vandana: two years, then apprenticeship. I want my own electrical business one day
Sunaina: then I'm your first customer. my fan has been making noises for a month 😅
Vandana: deal. after I pass the safety module 🙂
Sunaina: proud of you 💪

qa.q: What course did Vandana enroll in at the ITI?
qa.a: The electrician course.

qa.q: How does Vandana feel about her decision?
qa.a: She is scared but certain, because working on the wiring made her feel alive in a way the BA classes never did.

qa.q: How could Vandana's mother be supported with her worries?
qa.a: Vandana could share what she learns and her business plan, and maybe introduce her to women already working in the trade.

grounding: Shows through a chat a young woman committing to a vocational trade path over a general degree.

passage: In the village, most boys Yogesh's age were leaving for city jobs. His cousin Ojas had gone to Mumbai and sent back photos of tall buildings. Yogesh, nineteen, stood at the edge of his father's sugarcane field one evening with the admission letter for a two-year agriculture diploma at the district college. His father had struggled for years with failing crops and falling water. Yogesh had seen the drip irrigation at the model farm on the highway and couldn't stop thinking about it. "You want to study farming?" his father asked, half laughing. "Papa, I want to learn how to farm better," Yogesh said. That night, he signed the form by lantern light, his heart thumping, and folded it into his shirt pocket for the morning bus.

qa.q: What did Yogesh see at the model farm on the highway?
qa.a: Drip irrigation.

qa.q: What does Yogesh's thumping heart show when he signs the form?
qa.a: He is nervous but determined, committing to a path different from the other boys and from what his father expected.

qa.q: How could Yogesh's father support his choice?
qa.a: He could share his own farming experience and let Yogesh try new ideas on a small part of the field as he learns.

qa.q: Why might Ojas react differently to Yogesh's choice?
qa.a: Having left for the city, Ojas may see farming as the old life, while Yogesh sees it as a future he can improve.

grounding: Shows a young man in a village committing to a specialised agricultural path to build a future on the family land.

passage: In the laundry room of her residence in Montreal, Rania, nineteen, held the form due on Friday: declare your major. She had taken intro psychology, economics and an art elective, and liked them all a little. Her roommate Camila folded towels beside her. 'Which one made you forget to eat?' Rania thought. It wasn't any of the classes. It was her weekend job at the bike co-op, rebuilding wheels, where three hours felt like ten minutes. 'That's not a major.' 'The college has a mechanical technology program,' Camila said. 'Two years. Hands-on.' Rania's stomach flipped: fear of disappointing her parents, and something like relief. That night she emailed the program advisor. On Friday she handed in the form with a new name written in.

qa.q: When was the form due?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rania have when Camila mentioned the program?
qa.a: She felt afraid of disappointing her parents and also relieved, as if a real fit had been named.

qa.q: What could Rania do to feel surer about her choice?
qa.a: She could talk with the advisor and current students, and explain her reasons to her parents calmly.

qa.q: How might Rania's parents react to her new path?
qa.a: They might be surprised or worried at first, but could come round if they see how committed and happy she is.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specific hands-on program after noticing where her real absorption lies.

passage: The electrical workshop at the ITI smelled of hot solder and dust. Kiran, twenty, finished wiring the practice board and flicked the switch; all four bulbs lit. Vijay Sir, the instructor, nodded but didn't smile. 'Your cousins are all doing BCom, no?' 'Yes, sir.' 'And you?' Kiran wiped his hands. For a year he had been half in, half out, thinking he might switch to a degree once the relatives stopped asking. 'I want the wireman licence,' he said. 'Then solar installation. I'm not switching.' He was surprised how steady his voice sounded. Vijay Sir finally smiled and handed him the form for the advanced solar module. 'Then stop coming late on Mondays.' Kiran laughed. 'Yes, sir.'

qa.q: How many bulbs lit when Kiran flicked the switch?
qa.a: All four.

qa.q: What did Kiran notice about his own voice, and what does it show about how he felt?
qa.a: He was surprised it sounded steady, which shows he felt sure of his choice after a year of doubt.

qa.q: How did Vijay Sir support Kiran's commitment?
qa.a: He gave him the form for the advanced module and also held him to a standard about punctuality.

qa.q: How might Kiran's relatives see his choice?
qa.a: Some may compare him with the cousins doing BCom, but they may come to respect a skilled trade.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult committing to a specific trade path at a training institute.

passage:
Dear Anand Mama,
I'm writing because I've decided something, and I want you to hear it from me. I'm leaving BCom after this year. I've spent two years in lectures I don't care about while spending every free hour in your workshop, sanding and joining wood. I've applied for the furniture design and carpentry course at the polytechnic. Papa is worried about money and status. I've made a plan: I'll work part-time at your workshop if you'll have me, and I'll show him the placement numbers. I'm scared. But when I'm making something, I feel like myself. Will you help me talk to him?
Ira

qa.q: Which course did Ira apply for?
qa.a: The furniture design and carpentry course at the polytechnic.

qa.q: How does Ira feel about the decision?
qa.a: Ira feels scared but sure, feeling most alive while making things.

qa.q: What makes Ira's plan more convincing?
qa.a: It has a concrete course, a part-time job idea and facts to show Papa, not just feelings.

qa.q: How might Anand Mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Touched and proud that Ira found a passion in his workshop, and a little worried about Papa.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specialised trade path and planning how to pursue it.

passage: Thanks, Preeti, for having me on your campus radio show. I'm Asif, twenty-one, final-year agriculture. People ask why I chose farming science when I could've done engineering. Honestly, I tried engineering prep for a year and felt nothing. Then during lockdown I was back in my village, watching my father lose half his tomato crop to a pest. I spent nights reading about soil and pests. I realised I wanted to understand this, not escape it. So I switched. Now I'm specialising in soil health. It's harder than I thought. But every lab test feels like it matters for someone like my father.

qa.q: What is Asif specialising in?
qa.a: Soil health.

qa.q: What did Asif feel watching his father lose half the tomato crop?
qa.a: Asif felt upset and helpless, and then driven to understand the problem.

qa.q: What turning point in Asif's story led to the specialisation?
qa.a: The lockdown months in the village, seeing the crop loss and reading about soil and pests.

qa.q: How might Asif's father see the career choice?
qa.a: Probably with pride, knowing the father's own struggle shaped this path.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specialised field after a personal turning point.

passage: I'm Pradeep, Hafsa's younger brother. For two years Hafsa, now twenty, drifted between courses: economics, then psychology, then back. Last summer she started volunteering with a local news website, writing about water shortages in our area. I'd never seen her so busy. She interviewed tanker drivers at six in the morning and wrote until midnight. In September she told our parents she was switching to journalism. There was an argument, but she had her articles printed out and ready. I don't know if she's sure, but she hasn't changed her mind since.

qa.q: What did Hafsa write about while volunteering?
qa.a: Water shortages in their area.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have felt while writing until midnight?
qa.a: She seemed energised and absorbed, finally caring deeply about her work.

qa.q: What would you advise Hafsa now that she has chosen journalism?
qa.a: Keep building a portfolio and find a mentor in the field to guide her next steps.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see his sister's change?
qa.a: He notices she's never been so busy and determined, though he can't be sure she's certain.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from drifting to committing to a career path, seen by her brother.

passage:
January: Ujjwal, twenty, sat through his second-year BCom accounting lecture doodling recipes in the margins. He'd been cooking dinner for his family since he was fourteen.
March: His sister Payal found him watching a video about a two-year culinary diploma. "You'd leave commerce?" "I don't know," he said. "Papa will freak." "What do you want?" Ujjwal looked at the screen. "This."
June: After a long talk with his parents, and a visit to the institute's kitchen, Ujjwal submitted his application. He felt terrified and sure at the same time. Payal took a photo of him holding the acknowledgement slip, grinning like an idiot.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal doodle in the accounting lecture?
qa.a: Recipes.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel after submitting the application?
qa.a: He felt terrified and sure at the same time.

qa.q: What steps helped Ujjwal commit to the new path?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Payal, then his parents, and visiting the institute's kitchen before applying.

qa.q: How might Payal feel taking the photo?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and proud of her brother for choosing what he wants.

grounding: Over six months, a young man moves from a commerce degree to committing to a culinary diploma.

passage: Rekha Mausi folded her hands. "Afreen, you're asking how I chose nursing? At nineteen, I was doing BSc chemistry because my father wanted it. One day my neighbour fell in the market, and I was the only one who stayed with her till the ambulance came. I held her hand. At the hospital, a nurse spoke to me so calmly, I thought: I want to be that. I went home and said, 'I'm switching.' My father didn't speak to me for a week. I did it anyway. The first year was hard, night shifts, exams, blisters. But I never once wished I'd stayed in chemistry." Afreen looked at her own application forms. "How did you know?" "I didn't. I chose, and then I kept choosing."

qa.q: What was young Rekha studying at nineteen?
qa.a: BSc chemistry.

qa.q: How did young Rekha feel when she watched the nurse speak calmly?
qa.a: She felt inspired and certain, wanting to be like that nurse.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Rekha, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: Staying with her fallen neighbour and seeing the nurse; switching cost her a week of her father's silence and a hard first year.

qa.q: How might young Rekha's father have felt about the switch?
qa.a: He was likely upset and disappointed at first, since he had wanted her to do chemistry.

grounding: An aunt recounts committing to nursing at nineteen, against her father's wishes.

passage: The university portal closed at midnight, and at ten the power went out in Shreya's Guwahati hostel. She had to choose her major: economics or psychology. Her phone was at twenty percent. Her roommate Noor lit a candle. "Just pick economics. Safer jobs." Shreya stared at the flame. She thought about the psychology elective she'd loved, the way she'd stayed up reading about memory for fun. Economics felt like a coat that didn't fit. "Psychology," she said. "But I'm scared." Noor handed her the phone hotspot. "Then be scared and submit." With the phone at eight percent, Shreya clicked submit at 11:42. She sat back, heart pounding. "I did it." Noor clapped softly in the dark.

qa.q: At what time did Shreya click submit?
What was Shreya feeling as she chose psychology?
qa.a: She felt scared but sure, choosing the subject she loved over the safer option.

qa.q: What helped Shreya decide under pressure?
qa.a: Remembering what she genuinely enjoyed and Noor's push to submit despite fear.

qa.q: How might Noor feel after Shreya submitted?
qa.a: Noor likely feels happy for her and glad to have helped.

grounding: Under time pressure during a power cut, a student commits to psychology over the safer economics.

passage:
Imran sat on the steps of the engineering college in Bengaluru with two forms. One for staying in mechanical. One for switching to architecture, the subject he'd drawn in the margins of every notebook.
His mother had said, "Mechanical is safe." His drawing teacher, Ganga ma'am from school, had said, "You come alive when you sketch."
He had spent a month on it: sitting in architecture studio classes, talking to seniors, looking at the fees and the extra year. He was scared. Architecture meant starting again, alone.
He called Ganga ma'am. "What if I regret it?"
"Then you'll learn from it. But what will you regret more?"
Imran signed the architecture form and sat very still, heart pounding.

qa.q: What had Imran drawn in the margins of every notebook?
qa.a: Architecture, the subject he had drawn in every notebook.

qa.q: How did Imran feel after signing the architecture form?
qa.a: He felt scared but determined, sitting still with his heart pounding.

qa.q: What did Imran do well before deciding?
qa.a: He spent a month testing the choice by sitting in studio classes, talking to seniors and checking fees and time.

qa.q: How might Imran's mother feel about his choice?
qa.a: She may feel worried about safety, but could come to accept it if she sees how much it means to him.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specialised field after weighing it carefully.

passage:
"You're sure? Nursing?" Jyoti asked, putting down her tea.
Kavitha nodded. "I did the hospital volunteering for three months. I liked every bit of it, even the night shifts."
"But you were topping in commerce."
"I was good at commerce. I wasn't happy in it."
"And Papa?"
"He's upset. He thinks nursing is too hard for too little money."
Jyoti was quiet. "Is he wrong?"
"About the hard part, no. About the rest, I don't care as much as I thought." Kavitha turned the cup in her hands. "I've applied to the four-year course. Only that one."
"No backup?"
"The backup is doing it well."
Jyoti smiled. "Okay, then. I'll help you pack."

qa.q: How long did Kavitha volunteer at the hospital?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: How does Kavitha seem to feel about her decision?
qa.a: She seems calm and resolved, though aware Papa is upset.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha before the course starts?
qa.a: Talk openly with Papa about why she chose nursing, and keep the mentors she met while volunteering.

qa.q: How is Jyoti affected by Kavitha's choice?
qa.a: Jyoti is surprised and a little worried at first, then supportive enough to offer to help pack.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing firmly to a vocational path despite family doubt.

passage:
I'm Lokesh. Three years ago I was doing a general science degree because everyone in my family did one.
In second year my friend Urmila dragged me to her uncle's carpentry workshop to pick up a chair. I stayed four hours. The smell of wood, the sound of the plane. I asked a hundred questions. Her uncle let me try a joint and I did it badly, and I was happy.
I dreamt about it for months. Then I looked up furniture design courses and woodworking diplomas. I talked to Urmila's uncle again, and to my parents, who were confused and then, slowly, curious.
I finished the degree and joined a one-year furniture-making course. It's hard. My hands are full of cuts. But when I walk into the workshop, I know I'm in the right room.

qa.q: Where did Urmila take Lokesh?
qa.a: To her uncle's carpentry workshop to pick up a chair.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel after doing a joint badly?
qa.a: Lokesh felt happy and absorbed, even though the joint was bad.

qa.q: Which steps helped Lokesh choose this path wisely?
qa.a: Lokesh tested the interest by talking to a carpenter, researching courses and bringing the parents along before committing.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel knowing her errand changed Lokesh's path?
qa.a: Urmila may feel surprised and pleased to have helped a friend find their work.

grounding: A young adult reflects on committing to a specialised trade after a general degree.

passage:
Career cell note, second-year BSc, Tuesday
Ritu came in torn between staying in chemistry and switching to a diploma in food technology. She'd made a two-column list but kept crossing things out. Her friend Sachin, who came with her, said, "She lights up in the canteen kitchen, not in the lab." Ritu laughed but didn't disagree. I asked what she does on free Sundays: she tests pickle recipes and records the acidity. I pointed out that she'd been doing food chemistry for years without calling it that. She sat back and went quiet. We agreed she'll shadow the food-tech lab for a week and talk it over with her parents on Saturday. She left with her list folded in her pocket instead of clutched in her hand.

qa.q: What does Ritu do on free Sundays?
qa.a: She tests pickle recipes and records the acidity.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she sat back and went quiet?
qa.a: She seemed struck and relieved, seeing that her hobby already pointed to a clear path.

qa.q: What makes the agreed next steps sensible?
qa.a: Shadowing the food-tech lab for a week and talking with her parents lets her test the choice in real life before committing.

qa.q: How does Sachin see Ritu's choice?
qa.a: Sachin has noticed her energy in the canteen kitchen and gently nudges her toward what makes her light up.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving toward committing to a specialised course, observed by a career counsellor.
